name: Traverses the String with a legal index/charAt loop vs. iterates the String directly with an enhanced for-loop (treats String as array/collection)
side_a: No deduct: the answer walks the String using an index-based loop with charAt/substring (or any construct that is legal on a String), even if the loop bounds, the off-by-one, or the mutation logic is wrong.
side_b: Deduct: the answer iterates the String object itself with an enhanced for-loop (e.g. `for (char c : username)`), which is not legal Java for a String and shows the traversal mechanism itself is not understood.

name: Uses only methods that actually exist on String vs. invokes a non-existent method on the String field
side_a: No deduct: all method calls on the String field are real String methods (charAt, substring, length, replace), even if the call is useless or its return value is discarded.
side_b: Deduct: the answer calls a method that does not exist on String (e.g. `username.delete(character)`), inventing API rather than misusing it.

name: Index value that runs off the end of the String (real bounds error) vs. merely malformed String-method call form
side_a: No_deduct when the String method call is only malformed in form (wrong argument order, wrong count, misspelled name) but every index the algorithm actually computes stays inside [0, length()-1] given the loop bounds, or is guarded before use (e.g., `i < username.length() - 1 && ...`). Sloppy call syntax alone is the excused 'calls a String method incorrectly' case.
side_b: Deduct when the loop bounds plus the index arithmetic make an access genuinely out of range — e.g., `charAt(i + 1)` evaluated when `i` can be the last index, or a loop condition `i <= username.length()`. This is a bounds error on a well-formed call, not a malformed call, so the excuse does not apply.

name: Builds and returns a newly constructed String vs. relies on mutating the String instance variable in place
side_a: No_deduct when the response accumulates the answer into a separate variable (String accumulator, StringBuilder) or assigns the result of an immutable String operation back before returning it, so the returned expression is a genuinely newly constructed string.
side_b: Deduct when the response treats the String field as mutable or as a collection/array — calling a mutator-style method whose result is discarded (`username.replace("-", "");`, `username.delete(...)`) or iterating it with an enhanced for loop as if it were char[] — so the value actually returned is the unmodified original (or an un-built accumulator). This is a defect in constructing the returned string, not an excusable call-form slip.
